A year group of 50 students is asked two questions. 27 play for a sports team, 18 play in the orchestra, and 7 put a hand up for both.
Add 27 and 18 and you get 45. But 12 of the 50 put no hand up at all, so fewer than 45 did at least one: the 7 were counted in each total.

noteBlocks.md:
In everyday speech 'or' can mean one or the other but not both. In probability it never does. $A$ **or** $B$ means at least one of them happens, and that includes the case where both happen.
So the group you want is the whole of both circles together, overlap included, written $A \cup B$ and read 'A union B'.

noteBlocks.md: Count the 'or' group region by region and nobody is counted twice: $20 + 7 + 11 = 38$. The two totals give $27 + 18 = 45$ instead.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the year group, 27 plus 18 comes to 45, but only 38 students do at least one. Why?
options: The 7 students in both groups are counted in each total
The 12 who do neither were added in by mistake
The two totals should have been multiplied
noteBlocks.answer: The 7 students in both groups are counted in each total
noteBlocks.explain: Each of those 7 appears once in the 27 and once again in the 18. Take them off once and 38 is left.

noteBlocks.text: 2. The rule your formula sheet gives you

noteBlocks.md:
Page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet prints $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Add the two probabilities, then subtract the overlap, $P(A \cap B)$, read 'A intersection B'. What is left is the probability of at least one.
Probabilities work the same way. If $P(A) = 0.55$, $P(B) = 0.25$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$, then $P(A \cup B)$ is $0.55 + 0.25 - 0.1 = 0.7$.

noteBlocks.title: Why subtract once and not twice?
noteBlocks.md: Every student in the overlap was counted exactly twice, once in $P(A)$ and once in $P(B)$. Subtracting the overlap once brings each back to a single count; subtract twice and they vanish from the answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: For the year group of 50, where 27 play for a sports team, 18 play in the orchestra and 7 do both, work out $P(\text{sports team or orchestra})$. Give a fraction or a decimal.
noteBlocks.explain: $\dfrac{27}{50} + \dfrac{18}{50} - \dfrac{7}{50}$ is $\dfrac{38}{50}$, which is 0.76. Leaving the overlap in would give 0.9.

noteBlocks.md:
Two events are **mutually exclusive** when they cannot both happen, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and the rule loses its last term.
A spinner with 8 equal sections has 3 red, 2 blue and 3 green. One spin cannot land red and blue at once, so $P(\text{red or blue}) = \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{2}{8}$, which is $\dfrac{5}{8}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which pair of events, for one student in a form group, is mutually exclusive?
options: Born in March, and born in July
Brings a packed lunch, and has a bus pass
noteBlocks.answer: Born in March, and born in July
noteBlocks.explain: Nobody has two birth months, so that overlap is empty. A student can do both of the other pairs, so each of those needs the subtraction.

noteBlocks.text: 4. See it done: a theatre group

noteBlocks.md:
A theatre group of 60 members: 31 act, 26 work backstage and 9 do both. One member is chosen at random.
**Step 1.** Name the events, because the rule is written in letters. $A$ is acting, $K$ is backstage.
**Step 2.** Write the three probabilities over the same total: $\dfrac{31}{60}$, $\dfrac{26}{60}$ and $\dfrac{9}{60}$.

**Step 3.** Put them into the rule: $\dfrac{31}{60} + \dfrac{26}{60} - \dfrac{9}{60}$.
The denominators already match, so only the numerators combine. That last line is yours, in the check below.

noteBlocks.title: The OR Rule
noteBlocks.why: A short run through adding probabilities. It works through mutually exclusive events; the subtraction for events that can both happen is the step this unit adds on top.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the theatre group of 60, 31 act, 26 work backstage and 9 do both. What is $P(\text{acts or works backstage})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
noteBlocks.explain: $\dfrac{31 + 26 - 9}{60}$ is $\dfrac{48}{60}$, which is $\dfrac{4}{5}$. The unreduced form earns the same mark.

noteBlocks.md:
**Or** means at least one, so you add and take the overlap off once.
**And**, for two events that do not affect each other, means multiply. If the chance of fog tomorrow is $0.2$, the chance of a frost is $0.35$ and the question says the two are independent, then $P(\text{both}) = 0.2 \times 0.35$, which is $0.07$. Fog and frost often come together, so only that sentence lets you multiply.

noteBlocks.title: The commonest way this is lost
noteBlocks.md: The 2022 report found many candidates adding two probabilities that the question needed multiplied, on one of the easier questions of the paper. Decide 'or' or 'and' in writing before you calculate.

noteBlocks.prompt: A bag holds red and blue beads. Which question needs $P(A) \times P(B)$ rather than the addition rule?
options: Two beads are taken, the first put back before the second is drawn. What is the probability that both are red?
One bead is taken. What is the probability that it is red or blue?
One bead is taken. What is the probability that it is not red?
noteBlocks.answer: Two beads are taken, the first put back before the second is drawn. What is the probability that both are red?
noteBlocks.explain: 'Both' is an 'and' question about two events in turn, and putting the first bead back leaves the second draw unchanged, so the two probabilities multiply. The other two are about one bead and need adding or subtracting.

noteBlocks.md:
The rule links four probabilities, so any one of them can be found from the other three. When the union is given, the overlap is $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$.
With $P(A) = 0.62$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$, that is $0.62 + 0.3 - 0.8 = 0.12$.

noteBlocks.explain: Rearrange the rule: $0.35 + 0.5 - 0.6 = 0.25$. The two probabilities add to more than the union by exactly the overlap.

noteBlocks.md: **'During' means at least one.** Summer 2026 asked for rain during a two-day weekend: rain on the Saturday, the Sunday or both, which is an 'or'. With $P(\text{Sat}) = 0.35$, $P(\text{Sun}) = 0.3$ and $P(\text{both}) = 0.1$, it is $0.35 + 0.3 - 0.1 = 0.55$.

**An answer above 1.** Summer 2019 examiners reported probabilities greater than 1: the overlap left in. $0.7 + 0.45 = 1.15$ can never be a probability, so a total like that means the overlap still has to come off.

noteBlocks.prompt: The chance of rain on Saturday is $0.45$, on Sunday $0.2$, and on both days $0.05$. What is the probability of rain during the weekend?
noteBlocks.explain: 'During the weekend' is at least one of the two days, an 'or': $0.45 + 0.2 - 0.05 = 0.6$.

The first mark is the three probabilities written over the same total; the last is the single fraction or decimal. Stuck: draw the two circles, fill the overlap first, and add the regions you need.

steps.decision: Name the events and write all three probabilities over the same total. The rule on the sheet is written in letters, so the letters have to mean something before it can be used.
Substitute into $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$. The last term is there because the 12 members who do both were counted in each of the first two.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on something you already know. A bag holds 5 red and 3 green beads. What is the probability that one bead taken at random is red?
items.skill: Probability from equally likely outcomes (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: 5 red out of 8 beads altogether. Every probability in this topic is built from a count like this.
That compares red with green rather than with the whole bag. The denominator is always the total number of outcomes, which is 8.
That is the probability of green. The question asked for red, so the numerator is 5.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. If $P(A) = 0.35$, what is the probability that $A$ does not happen?
items.skill: The complement of an event (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: the two possibilities total 1, so the complement is $1 - 0.35$. You will use this to turn 'at least one' into 'neither'.
A probability is never negative. Take 0.35 away from 1 instead of from 0.
That is the probability that $A$ does happen. The complement is what is left of the whole: $1 - 0.35$.

items.stem: One more from earlier work, before anything new. In a group of 30 people, 12 wear glasses. What fraction of the group wear glasses, in its simplest form?
items.skill: Writing a count as a fraction of a total and simplifying (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: $\dfrac{12}{30}$ cancels by 6. Either form earns the mark in the exam, and the unsimplified one is often easier to keep working with.
18 is the number who do not wear glasses. The denominator of a probability is the whole group, which is 30.
That is the fraction upside down, and it is larger than 1. A probability sits between 0 and 1.

items.stem: In a class of 25, 14 play a team sport, 11 play an instrument and 6 do both. How many play at least one of the two?
items.skill: Counting a union from two totals and an overlap

options.feedback: Yes: $14 + 11 - 6 = 19$. The 6 in both were counted in each total, so they come off once.
That is $14 + 11$, with the 6 who do both counted twice. Taking them off once leaves 19.
The 6 have been added rather than subtracted, so they are now counted three times. The rule subtracts the overlap: 19.

items.stem: $P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and the two events are mutually exclusive. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
items.skill: The addition rule when the overlap is empty

options.feedback: Yes. Mutually exclusive means $P(A \cap B) = 0$, so the rule's last term is zero and the two probabilities simply add.
That is $0.6 \times 0.3$, which answers 'both'. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so multiplying is never the route here.

That takes $0.6 \times 0.3 = 0.18$ off as the overlap, as if the events were independent. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so the overlap is empty and nothing comes off: $0.6 + 0.3 = 0.9$.

items.stem: A card is drawn from an ordinary pack. Which pair of events is NOT mutually exclusive?
items.skill: Recognising when two events can happen together

options.text: The card is a heart; the card is a queen
options.feedback: Yes: the queen of hearts is both, so the overlap is not empty and the addition rule needs its last term.

options.text: The card is a heart; the card is a spade
options.feedback: No card is in two suits at once, so these two cannot happen together and the overlap is empty.

options.text: The card is a king; the card is a seven
options.feedback: A card carries one value, so it cannot be a king and a seven. That overlap is empty too.

items.stem: A coin is tossed and a dice is rolled. Which calculation gives the probability of a head AND a six?
items.skill: Telling an 'and' question from an 'or' question

options.feedback: Yes: the two are independent, so 'and' multiplies. That gives $\dfrac{1}{12}$.
Adding answers 'a head or a six'. Examiners reported this exact swap on a straightforward opening question in 2022: decide 'and' or 'or' in writing before calculating.
That is the addition rule, which gives 'a head or a six'. For both together the two probabilities multiply.

parts.stem:
The Venn diagram shows the 40 students in a form group.
Write down how many students have a bus pass but do not bring a packed lunch.
hints: The bus-pass circle holds two regions.
Use the region outside the overlap.
parts.workedSolution:
The bus-pass circle holds 8 in the overlap and 7 outside it, and 8 + 7 = 15.
So 7 students have a bus pass only.

context.setting: A form group asked about packed lunches and bus passes

parts.stem:
In a form group of 40 students, 22 bring a packed lunch, 15 have a bus pass and 8 do both.
One student is chosen at random.
Calculate the probability that this student brings a packed lunch or has a bus pass.
hints: Add the two totals, then take the overlap off once.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $\dfrac{22 + 15}{40}$, with the 8 students in both counted twice. The rule takes the overlap off once, leaving $\dfrac{29}{40}$.
The two probabilities have been multiplied, which answers 'brings a packed lunch and has a bus pass' for two independent picks. 'Or' adds and then takes the overlap off: $\dfrac{29}{40}$.

context.setting: A form group asked about packed lunches and bus passes

parts.stem:
In the same form group of 40 students, 22 bring a packed lunch, 15 have a bus pass and 8 do both.
Calculate the probability that a student chosen at random does neither.
hints: Find the probability of at least one first.
Everything left over sits outside both circles.
parts.workedSolution:
At least one: $\dfrac{22 + 15 - 8}{40} = \dfrac{29}{40}$.
Neither is what is left: $1 - \dfrac{29}{40} = \dfrac{11}{40}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both totals have been taken off the class without the overlap being put back, so the 8 in both were removed twice. Find at least one first, $\dfrac{29}{40}$, then subtract from 1 to reach $\dfrac{11}{40}$.

context.setting: Customers at a village bakery choosing a scone or a traybake

parts.stem:
On one morning 50 customers came into a village bakery. 28 bought a scone, 20 bought a traybake and 11 bought both.
One of those customers is picked at random.
Calculate the probability that this customer bought a scone or a traybake.
hints: The 11 who bought both appear in each total.
Add, then subtract the overlap once.

commonErrors.feedback: The 11 customers who bought both are still counted twice. Taking them off once gives $\dfrac{37}{50}$.
Multiplying answers a different question. 'Or' means at least one of the two, so add the probabilities and take the overlap off: $\dfrac{37}{50}$.

context.setting: Two features of a randomly chosen library card record

parts.stem:
For a library card chosen at random, $P(A) = 0.42$, $P(B) = 0.35$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.18$.
Calculate $P(A \cup B)$.
hints: The rule is printed on page 2 of the booklet.
Substitute the three numbers straight in.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $P(A) + P(B)$ with the intersection still counted twice. The rule's last term takes $0.18$ off once, giving $0.59$.
The two probabilities have been multiplied. $P(A \cup B)$ adds them and then removes the overlap: $0.59$.

context.setting: A weather forecast for a gardening day

parts.stem:
A forecast gives the probability of rain tomorrow as $0.3$ and the probability of a strong wind as $0.45$. The two are independent.
Calculate the probability that tomorrow brings both rain and a strong wind.
hints: 'Both' asks for two things to happen together.
parts.workedSolution:
The events are independent, so $P(\text{rain and wind}) = 0.3 \times 0.45$.
$= 0.135$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two probabilities have been added. Adding answers 'rain or wind'; 'both' asks for the two together, so multiply: $0.135$.

context.setting: Singers in a community choir who sing alto, soprano or both

parts.stem:
A community choir has 60 singers. 27 sing alto, 38 sing soprano and 14 sing in both sections.
One singer is chosen at random.
Calculate the probability that this singer sings alto or soprano.
You must show your working.
hints: Take the 14 in both sections off once.

commonErrors.feedback: The answer is above 1, which no probability can be: the 14 singers in both sections were counted twice. Taking them off once gives $\dfrac{17}{20}$.
The two probabilities have been multiplied. 'Or' adds them and removes the overlap once: $\dfrac{17}{20}$.

parts.stem: Calculate the probability that the singer chosen sings in neither section.
hints: Everyone either sings in at least one section or in neither.

commonErrors.feedback: A negative answer means part (a) came out above 1, with the 14 in both sections counted twice. Fix the union first, then $1 - \dfrac{17}{20} = \dfrac{3}{20}$.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked for the probability that a student chosen from a form group of 40 brings a packed lunch or has a bus pass. 22 bring a packed lunch, 15 have a bus pass and 8 do both. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 adds the two probabilities and stops. The 8 students who do both are inside each total, so they have been counted twice. The rule on the formula sheet has a third term for exactly this: subtract $P(\text{both}) = 8/40$ once.
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 is right, but the method mark is for the whole rule with the overlap taken off, so both marks go at line 2, where the 8 stay counted twice. A quick check would have caught it: 0.925 is close to 1 for a group where 11 students do neither. The answer is $\dfrac{29}{40}$.

prompts.prompt: The addition rule for two events, as the Unit 3 formula sheet prints it.
What does 'or' mean in a probability question, and what does it include?
prompts.answer: At least one of the two events happens, and that includes the case where both happen.

prompts.prompt: What does it mean for two events to be mutually exclusive, and what does the addition rule become?
prompts.answer: They cannot both happen, so the intersection is empty and P(A and B) = 0. The rule becomes P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

prompts.prompt: How do you decide whether to add or to multiply two probabilities?
prompts.answer: Or means at least one, so add and take the overlap off once. And means both together, so for independent events multiply.

prompts.prompt: Why does the addition rule take the overlap off once?
prompts.answer: Anyone in both events is counted in P(A) and again in P(B), so the overlap is counted twice.
